name: complacency
quote: She seems kind of stuck at that level.
description: A sense that someone is more satisfied about their situation than they should be. That they could and should be doing more in some area.
perceptions: There's something that person should be considering.
They seem satisfied with the status quo or don't seem to be aware of what they're missing.
I think they should be doing more.
examples: A gardener who accepts insect damage when maybe they could plant bug repellant herbs.
A student who's happy with a B when they could get an A if they worked a little harder.

guidance.description: From the inside, it can be difficult to balance 'satisfaction' and 'complacency'. Sometimes accepting some part of your situation might be healthier than stressing about it.
If you feel that you or someone important to you is letting something important slip by, here are some references.

variations.name: underappreciation
variations.description: A sense that someone doesn't notice something that they should, or value something as much as they should.
perceptions: There's something that person doesn't seem to be valuing appropriately.
They don't seem to be aware of what they're neglecting.
I think they should be doing more.
examples: A person who complains about one aspect of their spouse, but doesn't praise an important positive.
Being hard on yourself about something while not recognizing a partial success.
Not taking good care of your houseplants.

comparisons.description: With 'underappreciate', the assumption is that the person is not aware of the value. With 'ingratitude', the person is aware of the value but feels entitled to it.

guidance.description: Displaying appreciation to someone includes gratitude, but also just interacting with someone and noticing small things. Here are some references that may be of interest.

comparisons.description: With 'laziness', there's an awareness that you should be doing the thing. With 'complacency', you're satisfied that thing isn't necessary.

commentaries.quote: The tragedy of life is often not in our failure, but rather in our complacency; not in our doing too much, but rather in our doing too little.
'If it ain't broke, don't fix it' is the slogan of the complacent, the arrogant or the scared. It's an excuse for inaction.

In the pursuit of a fulfilling life, two concepts often find themselves at odds: contentment and complacency. While on the surface, these words may appear similar, they represent vastly different states of mind and being. Contentment is essential to living a rich life where one is liberated from insecurities and savor their achievements, while complacency is murky prison of fear, inaction and stagnation.
People don’t notice the things we do for them until we stop doing them.
It is really sad that those who really do contribute to the community are not thanked a lot, and those who are living off of society's expense are celebrated.
